events.title: Seathan born to the keeper's hearth
events.body: Seathan is born at Tobar dhìreach, the only son of the keeper of the fire coal and the rainbow, and has the fire coal in his hands from earliest childhood as every child of that hearth has had it before him.

events.title: Seathan takes the bag over
events.body: On his father's death Seathan takes the bag of two coals and the keeping in his twentieth year, and chooses, unlike his father before him, to keep the fire coal near the hearth rather than carry it abroad.

events.title: Seathan marries Caitir
events.body: Seathan takes Caitir, of a household two valleys east that keeps no coal of its own, and she comes to Tobar dhìreach knowing she marries a keeper and not only a husband.

events.title: The fire coal put into the pot itself
events.body: Seathan puts the fire coal into the fire the line holds to be the mason's own, carried unbroken since the night of the lightning, and it lies dark and cool through the flame as it lies in every other fire he has tried.

events.title: Seathan snaps his fingers on the doorstone
events.body: On a warm evening Seathan, breaking the fire coal into dust between his fingers and thinking of the mason and the lightning's crack, snaps his fingers without meaning to try anything, and the dust on his hand takes fire, red-gold, and leaves no mark on him.

events.title: Seathan laughs until Caitir comes
events.body: Seathan sits on the doorstone laughing until his wife comes out to him, and tells her, before he tells anyone else, that the fire has been in his own hand the whole thirty years he carried it.

events.title: The telling at the hearth
events.body: Seathan tells the fire coal's waking at the recital on the night of the lightning that same year, plainly, as he told it to Caitir, and the valley begins to call the sixth coal gual teine, the fire coal.

events.title: Caitir turns Seathan's hand over
events.body: Caitir, coming to the door at Seathan's shout with her hands floury from baking, sits down beside him on the doorstone and turns his hand over herself to see that there is no mark on it.

events.title: The children carry the fire coal's waking to their mother's kin
events.body: Seathan's children, having seen their father laughing on the doorstone, run to tell their mother's kin before they rightly understand what there is to tell, and the word goes to every hearth within a day's walk.

events.title: The rainbow thrown into the northern sea again
events.body: Seathan carries the rainbow coal to the northern shore in the old custom and throws it into the swell, and wades in after it to find it as dark and salt-wet as it went in.

events.title: Dressed-up tellings of the snap corrected
events.body: Tellers far from Tobar dhìreach begin to have Seathan snap his fingers on purpose, as a fisherman tries a new knot, and are corrected by those nearer the hearth who heard from Caitir that there was no purpose in it.

events.title: The rainbow tried at the river crossing
events.body: Seathan and Caitir carry the rainbow coal down to the crossing where the silver still burns under the current, and hold it and then throw it, and it lies cold and ordinary among the wet stones the next morning.

events.title: Caitir's saying of the rainbow
events.body: Caitir says, after the river trial, that the rainbow holds every spirit and so belongs wholly to none of them, a saying that afterward passes among Clann na Ceiste.

events.title: Caitir goes with the rainbow to the sea and the river
events.body: Caitir walks with Seathan to the northern shore and to the river crossing with the rainbow coal, the only keeper's wife of the line remembered to have gone and not stayed by the pot.

events.title: Seathan dies at his own hearth
events.body: Seathan dies in his three-and-seventieth year at Tobar dhìreach, the fire-pot burning near him, asking at the last to hold the fire coal once more rather than the rainbow.

events.title: The bag passes to Seathan's eldest son
events.body: The bag, holding only the rainbow now, passes from Seathan's grave to his eldest son, a quiet man who never expected so great a charge while his father's hand was still warm.

events.title: Caitir tries the rainbow once more
events.body: Caitir, staying on at Tobar dhìreach after Seathan's death, tries the rainbow once more at the river for the comfort of doing something with it, and it lies as dark and unmoved as it lay in her husband's hand.

events.title: Caitir dies at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: Caitir dies in her three-and-seventieth year, the same age Seathan reached before her, and is buried beside him near the slab.

events.title: Caitir tries the rainbow once more at the river
events.body: In the years after Seathan's death Caitir tries the rainbow once more at the river below the house, and puts it back in the bag without disappointment, having ceased to expect it to answer a woman who only wished it well.

events.title: The crowd at the column grows
events.body: Word of the fire coal's waking spreads beyond the hill country's own hearths, and people begin coming to Achadh a' Chalbh in tens and then in hundreds to hear the recital said at the column, camping about the stone rather than passing it by.

events.title: A nephew of Seathan afraid of the crowd
events.body: The young nephew of Seathan sent to say the Line at the column sits apart from the fires the day before, sick with fear of so many faces, until an old woman tells him that a story kept in one hearth is safe from nothing but changing.

events.title: The first shelters built at the column
events.body: The crowd that gathers to hear the recital builds the first low walls of turf and hide about Achadh a' Chalbh, taken down again when the telling ends, because no one yet thinks of the column's ground as a place a person lives.

events.title: Seathan's nephew gives the telling to a crowd
events.body: Clann na Ceiste sends a nephew of Seathan's to Achadh a' Chalbh to say the recital naming the fire coal to a hillside of strangers rather than a single hearth, and an old woman of the gathering tells him a story given to a crowd is safe from dying, whatever changes it gathers in the carrying.

events.title: The telling slowed for the crowd
events.body: For the crowd at the column the Line comes to be said more slowly, with a pause after each father's name long enough for those at the back to have it passed forward mouth to mouth.

events.title: The shelters at the column rebuilt
events.body: The shelters at Achadh a' Chalbh are rebuilt so many times over on the footings of the ones before them that a household coming for the first time can see, in the worn hollows and packed earth, that others have stood there before it and will stand there after.

events.title: The rainbow passed hand to hand at the column
events.body: At a great telling at the column a keeper of the bag gives the rainbow coal into the crowd, and it goes round from hand to hand by firelight through the whole night and comes back to him at dawn as dark as it went out.

events.title: The bag passes down the line of fathers
events.body: The bag holding the rainbow coal, gual bogha-froise, passes down the line of fathers from Seathan's son, and a keeper whose name the recital keeps from strangers resolves to try it in the oak grove at Doire ghlas.

events.title: The rainbow tried in the grove
events.body: A keeper of Clann na Ceiste carries the rainbow coal north to the oak grove at Doire ghlas and sits with it through a night by his own small fire as Diarmad once sat, waiting for any sign the Keeper gave before; the coal lies black and cold among the ash by morning, and the grove answers him nothing.

events.title: Aoife's child born
events.body: Aoife bears a living child after two she has already lost in their first winters, and lets herself believe, when it survives its own first winter thin but breathing steadily, that this one will live to walk; she sews it, for the first time, a coat cut to its own growing rather than one handed down.

events.title: Aoife sews a coat cut to the child's growing
events.body: Aoife, trusting for the first time that a child of hers will live, sews in the last cold months a small coat cut to the child's own growing, a thing she had not let herself do for the two children before.

events.title: Aoife's child dies
events.body: Aoife's child sickens in the spring and dies quietly in her arms, the third child she has lost and the first she does not hear cry out at the end, so that she says afterward she knew, before she was willing to know it, that this death would not be like the others.

events.title: The child buried with the sliver of coal
events.body: Aoife closes into her dead child's hand the one sliver of the coloured coal her household still keeps, over her husband's mother's objection, and it is buried with the child at the western edge of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the only piece of the vein put into the ground with the dead this age.

events.title: Words between two households over the sliver
events.body: Aoife's husband's mother says a hearth ought not give a piece of the coloured coal to the dead while the living have use for it, and there are words between the two households that neither afterward cares to keep.

events.title: The graves begin to keep a line
events.body: The newer graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach's western edge begin, without any household deciding it, to be set in a row facing the northern mountains, each new grave drawn to the line the ones before it have already kept, until a household bringing its dead looks for the row before it looks for empty turf.

events.title: A grave dug round an old swelling
events.body: A young man digging his grandfather's grave at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach proposes levelling an old unnamed swelling in his row's path, and is rebuked by an elder digger, who tells him no man may open a grave whose occupant he cannot name; the row bends round it instead.

events.title: An uncle forbids the levelling of an old grave
events.body: A young man digging his grandfather's grave at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach proposes to level an old swelling in the row's path, and his uncle forbids it: a man who cannot say whose grave he opens has no business opening it.

events.title: Aoife dies
events.body: Aoife dies in her seventieth year, forty years after burying her child, and is carried to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach and laid in the row nearest the western edge where the child already lies, the row bending as it reaches her grave to keep clear of the old swelling beside it.

events.title: The western face of the burial hill woven with bending rows
events.body: Seen from far enough off, the whole western face of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach shows no longer straight lines but a slow curved weaving of rows folding round the swellings no living hand made.

events.title: Beithir finds the cats' road in the snow
events.body: A herder of the central mountains follows three strayed ewes into a high saddle and finds a line of prints worn into the frozen turf on both sides of it, running straight where the ground gave the beast no cause to turn; his own hearth's elders tell him their fathers knew the same line and the same two turns of year it is kept in.

events.title: An old man tells Beithir the cats keep their roads
events.body: The oldest man of Beithir's hearth tells him that his father and his father's father said the same of that saddle: the great cats of the mountains do not wander the high ground but cross it, at some seasons and not others.

events.title: The gatepost sign first cut
events.body: A household of the high valleys cuts a fresh mark into its gatepost at the turn of year the cats' smell and track return to the passes, and scrapes it away again once both are gone, so that a stranger walking the crossing weeks can read the closed season on every post without asking what the mark means.

events.title: The shielings of the pass stand empty
events.body: The herders' summer camps on the high passes are found stripped and shuttered at the same point in every year while the cats cross, a boy sent up in error by his father's lost count of days finding one already closed and coming down again with nothing worse than a wasted night's walk.

events.title: The gatepost cut deep enough to read in the scraping
events.body: An old woman of the eastern slopes tells a new-married daughter that the crossing mark must be cut deep enough to be read even after it is scraped, so that a late-comer knows the season has been kept there before.

events.title: A boy sent up in error to a stripped shieling
events.body: A boy sent up to winter sheep at a shieling in the crossing season, his father having lost the count of days in a wet spell, finds it already stripped and shuttered by households that read the signs, and comes down the same evening.

events.title: Thirty head lost to a broken custom
events.body: A herdsman of the lower slopes, trusting his own count of the year over his neighbours' gatepost signs, keeps his cattle ten days past the crossing's start and brings them down to find thirty head missing from the herd, torn on the ground above the track in a way no wolf of that country tears ground.

events.title: The cats turn back at the foothills
events.body: A family watching from a rise above the track sees the crossing cats turn from the eastern passes and go back down toward the western foothills for no cause the watchers can find, and the country reads the plain sign as a warning rather than let it pass unanswered.

events.title: The households store double
events.body: On the strength of the turning cats the country stores double against a hard winter that no other sign has yet shown, cutting peat and laying by grain and dried meat past what the ordinary count of mouths at each hearth calls for; the winter that follows proves hard enough to repay the extra carrying.

events.title: The hard winter after the cats turned back
events.body: The winter after the cats turn back lays snow to a grown man's waist in the lower valleys for the better part of two months, and every household that stored double says afterward the cutting and the carrying were worth it.

events.title: A household scrapes its gatepost early
events.body: A household near the high passes, reading the geese's lateness as a slow season, scrapes its crossing mark bare a full ten days before the cats' smell returns to the saddle above it.

events.title: Cairbre and ten set out
events.body: Cairbre leads ten men inland from Teallaichean a' Chladaich, reasoning by the coast's own geese, which have not yet gone over in their numbers that autumn, that the crossing season has not yet begun; a household nearer the mountains has scraped its own gatepost clean on the same late reading and by the same error.

events.title: The eleven do not come home
events.body: Cairbre and the ten who went with him fail to reach the valley they set out for and do not return to the shore; no household along the mountains can say it saw them pass, and winter closes the high ground before any search can be made of it that year.

events.title: Word comes of a failed harvest inland
events.body: Word reaches Teallaichean a' Chladaich that kin settled two valleys further into the hills than the shore's people commonly go have had their harvest fail badly enough that they will not see the winter through unhelped, and Cairbre resolves to lead ten of his own hearth up to carry it down to them.

events.title: Suibhne born at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: A son is born to the household that keeps the fire-pot and the bag of coals, a big child who closes his hand round a finger held out to him and will not readily let it go, so that they say of him he was born holding on; he is given the name Suibhne.

events.title: Cairbre's wife watches the path thirty days
events.body: Cairbre's wife keeps the twelfth day and the fourteenth and the twentieth on the rise above Teallaichean a' Chladaich, and by the thirtieth has stopped telling herself anything, and only watches.

events.title: Two springs of searching find nothing
events.body: The shore and the kin the eleven had set out to help each try the high ground in the spring after they go missing, and again the spring after that, and both times come down with nothing to show for the walking but blistered feet and a country too wide to give up eleven men for the asking.

events.title: Suibhne learns the Line standing
events.body: Suibhne, a boy of the keeper's hearth, hears the whole of the Line said over him standing, as every keeper before him had heard it, and learns it.

events.title: The bones found along the cats' line
events.body: A drover's dog worries a length of bone out of the turf off the marked track at the proper close of a crossing season, and searchers over the following days gather a scatter of bone strung along roughly the same course the cats are known to keep, with nothing of what the eleven carried found among it.

events.title: The eleven buried where they were found
events.body: Unable to say with certainty which bones belonged to which man, the southern shore buries the gathered dead together high on the mountain rather than divide them wrongly among separate graves, and keeps alongside Cairbre's name the plainer lesson the country had already made of the matter: that the crossing months keep a count of their own that no household's calendar has yet learned to keep exactly with it.

events.title: Ailean born to Tobar dhìreach
events.body: A son is born to Suibhne of Clann na Ceiste at Tobar dhìreach, heavier in arm and leg than the women at his birth can readily match against memory, and slow to close his hand on a finger held out to him and slower to let it go, so that his mother says he was born holding on.

events.title: Ailean found by the fire-pot for whole mornings
events.body: Ailean, able to sit upright, is found by the fire-pot for whole mornings together, not reaching for it or troubling it, only sitting near enough to feel its heat and watching the low flame.

events.title: Ailean grows slow of speech and broad of hand
events.body: Ailean keeps to single words while children a season younger than him are stringing sentences, and some of his kin wonder aloud whether the line has thrown up a son too plain for the keeping, until his mother points to his hands, already broad at six years old, as proof enough of what manner of man he will be.

events.title: Ailean's mother answers the talk of his slowness
events.body: Ailean's mother puts a stop to the kin's talk of a son too plain for the keeping, saying a slow tongue is no mark against a steady hand, and pointing to his hands.

events.title: Suibhne drops the rainbow from Binnean a' Chlachair
events.body: In the second year of his keeping Suibhne climbs Binnean a' Chlachair and drops the rainbow from the height of his arm over the same steep side Fearghas used, and it falls to the stones without a flicker.

events.title: Suibhne lays the rainbow beside the burning silver
events.body: Suibhne throws the rainbow into the river at the crossing where the silver still burns under the current, so that for a breath the two lie side by side, dark against bright, before the current carries it on.

events.title: Suibhne will not try the rainbow by blood
events.body: Suibhne tries the rainbow by the sea, the height, the river and the earth, but will not try it by blood, telling his wife a man ought not open his own hand for a coal that has shown it wants no single element.

events.title: Suibhne carries the rainbow to Doire ghlas
events.body: In his four-and-fortieth year Suibhne walks the three days north to Doire ghlas with the rainbow coal, the first keeper to bring it to the grove where the Keeper first spoke, and sits under the oaks a night and a day with it held loose in his open hand; it shows him no change of colour or warmth, and he carries it home cold.

events.title: Suibhne says he doubts the rainbow will answer him
events.body: Suibhne tells his own hearth, and not the recital, that he no longer knows whether a man ought to go on asking a question already asked in every way his own life can think to ask it; his son Ailean, sixteen years old, hears it among the last things of any length his father says on the matter.

events.title: Ailean marries Lìobhan
events.body: Ailean, seventeen, takes Lìobhan of a household two valleys west that keeps no coal of its own; she comes to Tobar dhìreach a bride of fifteen and is taught by Suibhne's widow, in the short time left to teach her, how the fire-pot is fed and the bag kept and what is and is not said of it to a stranger.

events.title: Suibhne dies of a fever
events.body: Suibhne dies in his forty-sixth year of a fever that takes him inside a fortnight, with Ailean, eighteen years old and already the broadest man of that hearth, sitting with him through the last nights; the bag of two coals passes to Ailean, though no word of keeping is said over him yet.

events.title: Gormshuil born
events.body: A daughter is born to Ailean and Lìobhan in the same wet autumn the household buries Suibhne, and is named Gormshuil for the blue of her eyes at birth, which her grandmother swears she has never seen come on so soon in any other child.

events.title: Lìobhan names the rainbow's want
events.body: Lìobhan says aloud to Ailean what he has half thought and not yet let himself say, that a coal made of every colour together may belong wholly to no single element, as a child of two households belongs wholly to neither; Ailean turns the thought over the whole of that winter until it settles into near certainty.

events.title: Ailean tells the recital he means to light the six again
events.body: At the recital in his three-and-twentieth year Ailean tells the reciters only that he means, in the year ahead, to light the six coals again by each one's own old way and carry them living to wherever the seventh might at last be answered; the reciters say they will wait to hear how it goes.

events.title: Ailean wakes the gold on the northern sea
events.body: Ailean carries a fresh piece of the vein's gold-sheened colour the day's road north to the shore and throws it into the autumn swell as Aodh once did; it takes fire bright gold on the water, and this time he wades in after it and carries it home still burning in a clay pot with a lid of turf.

events.title: Ailean wakes the snowflake off the height
events.body: Before winter closes Binnean a' Chlachair, Ailean climbs it in a bitter wind and lets the snowflake coal fall from the height of his own arm as Fearghas once let it fall; it catches fire white halfway down the steep side, and he carries both fires down off the summit together.

events.title: Ailean wakes the black coal in the earth
events.body: In the last week before the ground freezes hard Ailean digs a grave-deep hole beside the old slab at Tobar dhìreach, lays the black coal in it as Brian once did, and finds it warm and glowing at dawn; three fires now burn under his roof through the shortest days of the year.

events.title: Ailean wades after the burning gold
events.body: Where Aodh let the gold burn out on the water, Ailean wades in to the waist after it and catches it still burning between his cupped hands, and carries it home in a clay pot with a turf lid.

events.title: Ailean sets out north with six fires on a pole
events.body: In the last week of an t-Iuchar Ailean sets out from Tobar dhìreach for Doire ghlas, carrying the six relit coals in clay pots slung from a pole across his shoulders and the dark rainbow coal wrapped against his chest, with Lìobhan and Gormshuil walking beside him as far as the last hearth before the moor.

events.title: Six fires kept under one roof
events.body: Through the last weeks of summer six fires burn in six clay pots under one roof at Tobar dhìreach for the first time since the making of the world, and Ailean wakes at odd hours to see that none has failed.

events.title: Ailean wakes the red-brown coal with his own blood
events.body: In the yard behind his house on a frosted spring morning Ailean sets the red-brown coal on a stone and strikes it as Cormac once struck his; the hammer turns and lays his hand open, and where his blood runs onto the coal a deep warm flame comes up, leaving a scar to match the byname's own.

events.title: Ailean wakes the silver in the Abhainn ghorm
events.body: At the crossing below Tobar dhìreach Ailean drinks from his own cupped hands as Eòghann once did and throws the silver coal into the current; it takes fire beneath the running water, and he lifts it out still alight with a wicker scoop made for the purpose.

events.title: Ailean wakes the fire coal on his own doorstone
events.body: Sitting on his doorstone at midsummer, thinking of nothing to do with fire, Ailean snaps his fingers over dust from the old fire coal without meaning to try anything, as Seathan once did by accident, and the dust flares red-gold and leaves no mark on him; the sixth fire is lit within the same year as the first five.

events.title: Gormshuil watches the lids lifted
events.body: Gormshuil, six years old, kept from the pots by her mother's word, is found more than once crouched at a safe distance watching the lids lifted on the six low fires in their six colours.

events.title: Lìobhan parts from Ailean at the last hearth
events.body: Lìobhan walks with Ailean as far as the last hearth before the moor with Gormshuil on her hip, and tells him only to mind his feet on the wet northern slopes and that she will keep the house fire until he comes home.
